chunks.text: Tomato Early Blight (Alternaria solani): Symptoms include circular to angular dark brown spots with concentric rings on older leaves. Yellow halos often surround spots. Severe infection causes defoliation. Favored by warm temperatures (24-29°C) and alternating wet and dry periods. Management: Remove infected leaves, practice crop rotation (avoid tomato/potato family for 2-3 years), ensure adequate plant spacing for airflow, mulch to prevent soil splash, avoid overhead irrigation.

Tomato Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans): Water-soaked lesions on leaves that turn brown-black. White sporulation visible on underside in humid conditions. Affects stems, petioles, and fruits. Spreads rapidly in cool (10-20°C), wet weather. Highly destructive. Management: Plant resistant varieties, improve field drainage, remove infected plants promptly, avoid leaf wetness. Consult local agricultural department for approved fungicide options.

Tomato Leaf Mold (Passalora fulva): Pale greenish-yellow spots on upper leaf surface with olive-green to gray-brown velvety growth on lower surface. Common in greenhouses and dense plantings with high humidity. Reduce humidity, improve ventilation, avoid overhead watering.

Tomato Bacterial Spot (Xanthomonas): Small water-soaked lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit. Lesions turn dark and irregular. Spread by rain splash and irrigation. Use certified disease-free seed, avoid working in wet fields, practice crop rotation.

Tomato Septoria Leaf Spot: Small circular spots with dark borders and gray-white centers. Tiny black dots visible in center of spots. Attacks lower leaves first. Avoid overhead irrigation, remove infected material, practice crop rotation.

Tomato Spider Mites (Two-spotted spider mite): Fine stippling and bronzing on leaves. Fine webbing visible. Worse in hot dry conditions. Improve plant water status, increase humidity, encourage natural predators.

Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus: Yellowing and upward curling of leaves, stunted plants, flower drop, reduced fruit set. Spread by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). Control whitefly populations, use reflective mulch, remove infected plants, plant resistant varieties.
Corn (Maize) Northern Leaf Blight (Exserohilum turcicum): Large tan cigar-shaped lesions on leaves. Lesions may have dark borders. Common in cool moist weather. Use resistant hybrids, rotate crops.

Corn Gray Leaf Spot (Cercospora zeae-maydis): Rectangular pale brown to gray lesions parallel to leaf veins. Favored by warm humid weather with extended dew periods. Use resistant varieties, crop rotation, reduce surface residue.
Corn Common Rust (Puccinia sorghi): Small cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces. Severe in cool moist weather. Use resistant hybrids.

Potato Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans): Water-soaked lesions on leaves, brown-black with white sporulation in humid conditions. Tuber rot can occur. Use certified seed, plant resistant varieties, improve drainage, avoid excessive irrigation.
Potato Early Blight (Alternaria solani): Similar to tomato early blight with dark concentric-ringed spots. Management includes crop rotation and removal of infected material.

Rice Blast (Magnaporthe oryzae): Diamond-shaped lesions with gray-white centers and brown borders on leaves. Can affect neck, panicle, and grain. Favored by high humidity, low light. Use resistant varieties, balanced fertilization, avoid excess nitrogen.

Powdery Mildew (various species): White powdery coating on leaf surfaces. Thrives in warm days and cool nights with high humidity but low rainfall. Improve airflow, avoid dense planting, avoid excess nitrogen fertilization.

Integrated Pest Management (IPM) is an ecosystem-based approach combining cultural, biological, mechanical, and chemical methods to minimize pest and disease damage. Steps: 1) Monitor crops regularly, 2) Identify pest/disease accurately, 3) Set action thresholds, 4) Apply preventive cultural controls first, 5) Use biological controls, 6) Apply chemical controls only when necessary and per label.

Soil testing is recommended before each crop season. Collect soil from multiple spots in the field at 0-15 cm depth. Send samples to nearest soil testing laboratory. Results guide fertilizer recommendations specific to your soil and crop.

Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone, reducing water use by 30-50% compared to flood irrigation. It also reduces foliar disease incidence by keeping leaves dry and can be combined with fertigation (applying fertilizers through irrigation water).

Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVK) are farm science centers established by ICAR across Indian districts. They provide: soil testing, seed distribution of improved varieties, pest and disease diagnosis, training programs, and direct demonstration of new technologies. Contact your nearest KVK for local crop-specific guidance.

PM-KISAN provides direct income support of Rs 6000 per year to eligible farmer families. eNAM is an online trading portal linking agricultural produce markets. PMFBY offers crop insurance at subsidized premiums.

Never apply pesticides during peak heat of the day (11am-3pm). Apply early morning or evening when wind speeds are low. Wear personal protective equipment including gloves, mask, and protective clothing. Never eat, drink, or smoke while handling pesticides. Store pesticides in original containers in locked storage, away from food and water sources.

Nitrogen deficiency shows as yellowing of older leaves starting from the bottom. Phosphorus deficiency causes purple coloration. Potassium deficiency causes leaf margin scorch. Conduct soil testing before applying any fertilizer.
Crop rotation helps break pest and disease cycles. Avoid planting the same crop family in the same field for consecutive seasons. Common rotation: cereals followed by legumes followed by vegetables.

Orange Citrus Greening (Huanglongbing): Asymmetric yellowing (blotchy mottle) on leaves; lopsided bitter fruit. Bacterial disease spread by Asian citrus psyllid. No cure exists. Control psyllid populations, remove and destroy infected trees, plant certified disease-free nursery stock.

Apple Scab (Venturia inaequalis): Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves and fruit surface. Favored by cool wet spring weather. Plant resistant varieties, remove fallen leaves, improve canopy airflow.

Grape Black Rot (Guignardia bidwellii): Brown lesions on leaves with black margins; black shriveled berries. During warm wet weather. Remove mummified berries, improve canopy management, avoid overhead irrigation.

Brown spots on crop leaves may indicate several conditions: early blight, late blight, septoria leaf spot, bacterial spot, or nutrient deficiencies. Upload a clear photograph of the affected leaf for more accurate AI-based detection. When symptoms started and weather conditions can help narrow the diagnosis.

If your crop leaves are turning yellow, possible causes include: nutrient deficiency (especially nitrogen), overwatering, root rot, viral infections, or natural senescence of older leaves. The pattern and location of yellowing helps distinguish causes. Consider soil testing.

For best results when photographing crop leaves for disease detection: use natural daylight (avoid direct sun glare), hold phone steady to avoid blur, capture both upper and lower leaf surfaces, include multiple affected leaves, ensure at least 3-4 clear spots visible in frame.
